quote: DeAngelis et al. (2015, Front. Microbiol.) report Actinobacteria, Alphaproteobacteria, and Acidobacteria as the phyla showing the strongest warming responses across 5/8/20-year warmed plots, with shifts most pronounced in the organic horizon — exactly what we see.
heading: Literature context

text: The report cites Pold et al. (2016, AEM) as showing that warming increases the fraction of carbohydrate-degrading genes affiliated with Actinobacteria.
quote: Pold et al. (2016, AEM) further show that warming increases the fraction of carbohydrate-degrading genes affiliated with Actinobacteria — a mechanistic complement to our compositional finding.
heading: Literature context

text: The report interprets its heated-mineral metabolite-richness decrease of 155 versus 167 ChEBI (p=0.012) as qualitatively consistent with published substrate-depletion models.
quote: Our heated-mineral metabolite-richness drop (155 vs 167 ChEBI, p=0.012) is qualitatively consistent with the substrate-depletion narrative emerging from these studies.
heading: Literature context

text: The report cites Melillo et al. (2017, Science) as documenting a 4-phase oscillating soil-C loss trajectory under +5°C warming.
quote: Melillo et al. (2017, Science) document a 4-phase oscillating soil-C loss trajectory under +5°C warming.
heading: Literature context

text: The report cites Domeignoz-Horta et al. (2022, GCB), studying 28-year warmed plots, as arguing that reduced substrate quantity and quality rather than thermal acclimation drives the apparent warming response.
quote: Domeignoz-Horta et al. (2022, GCB) — the closest temporal analog (28-year warmed plots) — argue that the apparent warming response is driven by **reduced substrate quantity and quality**, not thermal acclimation.
heading: Literature context

text: Roy Chowdhury et al. (2021) is identified as the closest published methodological precedent, using Harvard Forest organic and mineral metatranscriptomes under heated and control treatments.
quote: **Metatranscriptome at the same site (Roy Chowdhury et al. 2021):** This is the closest published methodological precedent — Harvard Forest metatranscriptomes (organic + mineral horizon, heated vs control).
heading: Literature context

text: The report states that Roy Chowdhury et al. found a larger treatment effect on KEGG transcripts than on CAZymes, with ~68% of differentially expressed CAZyme transcripts upregulated in heated soils.
quote: They report that **treatment had a larger effect on KEGG transcripts than on CAZymes**; ~68% of differentially expressed CAZyme transcripts were upregulated in heated soils.
heading: Literature context

text: The report describes its comparable DNA and RNA response (10-13% R²) as in tension with Roy Chowdhury et al.'s larger transcript-level effect, but cautions that sampling timepoint, replication, and analytical pipeline differ.
quote: Our finding that DNA and RNA respond comparably (10-13% R²) is in tension with their report of larger transcript-level effect, but the comparison is complicated by their different sampling timepoint, replication, and analytical pipeline.
heading: Literature context

text: The report describes Roy Chowdhury et al.'s upward CAZyme response as consistent with its chitinase up-result.
quote: Worth noting: their CAZyme up-direction is consistent with our chitinase up-result.
heading: Literature context

text: The report cites Choudoir et al. (2025, mSphere) as finding heated-plot Harvard Forest isolate genomes enriched in central carbohydrate and N metabolism and having reduced codon usage bias.
quote: **Pangenome-level adaptation (Choudoir et al. 2025, mSphere):** Pangenomes of Harvard Forest isolates show heated-plot genomes are enriched in central carbohydrate and N metabolism and show reduced codon usage bias — relevant to interpreting our DNA-level Actinobacteria enrichment as not just a compositional shift but a sub-clade selection.
heading: Literature context

text: The report interprets published Harvard Forest isolate pangenome adaptation as relevant to viewing its DNA-level Actinobacteria enrichment as sub-clade selection rather than only a compositional shift.
quote: Pangenomes of Harvard Forest isolates show heated-plot genomes are enriched in central carbohydrate and N metabolism and show reduced codon usage bias — relevant to interpreting our DNA-level Actinobacteria enrichment as not just a compositional shift but a sub-clade selection.
heading: Literature context

text: The report cites Zhang et al. (2024) as a precedent for methanotrophy under subtropical forest +4°C warming, where net CH₄ uptake increased 12-61% across soil depths and high-affinity USCα methanotroph relative abundance rose at 0-10 cm.
quote: **Methanotrophy as a forest-warming response (Zhang et al. 2024):** Our pmoA/pmoB upregulation in both horizons is unexpected for an aerated temperate forest but published in subtropical forest +4°C warming experiments, where net CH₄ uptake increased 12-61% across soil depths and the relative abundance of high-affinity USCα methanotrophs rose at 0-10 cm.
heading: Literature context

text: The report interprets the methanotrophy precedent as supporting the hypothesis that warming-induced moisture decrease increases CH₄ availability to methanotrophs.
quote: This supports the interpretation that warming-induced moisture decrease (a known concomitant of soil warming) increases CH₄ availability for methanotrophs.
heading: Literature context

text: The report cites Aliyu et al. (2016) for coordinated icl/aceA + aceB/glcB upregulation as a published Actinobacteria signature of stress or C2-substrate utilization.
quote: **Glyoxylate cycle activation under stress (Aliyu et al. 2016):** Coordinated icl/aceA + aceB/glcB upregulation is a published signature of stress / C2-substrate-utilization in Actinobacteria.
heading: Literature context

text: The report describes the heated-mineral RNA glyoxylate signature and Actinobacteria enrichment at Harvard Forest as mechanistically self-consistent.
quote: The fact that we see this in the heated-mineral RNA pool, in a Harvard Forest soil where Actinobacteria are enriched (Pold et al. 2016 + our data), is mechanistically self-consistent.
heading: Literature context

text: To its knowledge, the report provides the first explicit paired-sample comparison of DNA-pool and RNA-pool warming-response variance at Harvard Forest.
quote: To our knowledge, this is the **first explicit comparison of DNA-pool and RNA-pool warming response variance** in a paired-sample design at Harvard Forest, including the H1 sensitivity check that demonstrates the apparent DNA-vs-RNA imbalance is largely a horizon × incubation artifact.
heading: Novel contribution

text: The report's H1 sensitivity check indicates that the apparent Harvard Forest DNA-versus-RNA imbalance is largely a horizon × incubation artifact.
quote: To our knowledge, this is the **first explicit comparison of DNA-pool and RNA-pool warming response variance** in a paired-sample design at Harvard Forest, including the H1 sensitivity check that demonstrates the apparent DNA-vs-RNA imbalance is largely a horizon × incubation artifact.
heading: Novel contribution

text: The report describes the methanotrophy-up and glyoxylate-up RNA signature as previously unreported at Harvard Forest, while noting published precedents elsewhere.
quote: The methanotrophy-up + glyoxylate-up RNA signature is a previously unreported gene-level pattern at this specific site, although both signatures have published precedents elsewhere.
heading: Novel contribution

text: The Harvard Forest warming study has a single timepoint (2017-05-24), preventing detection of seasonal effects that Shinfuku et al. 2024 show are substantial at this site.
quote: - **Single timepoint** (2017-05-24). Cannot detect seasonal effects (which Shinfuku et al. 2024 show are substantial at this site).
heading: Limitations

text: The Harvard Forest warming study's omics sample sizes (n=28 metagenome, n=39 metatranscriptome) limit per-KO FDR power across 12-14K KOs.
quote: - **Sample size** for omics-rich layers (n=28 metagenome, n=39 metatranscriptome) limits per-KO FDR power across 12-14K KOs.
heading: Limitations

text: The Harvard Forest metatranscriptome KO data from contig annotations measure transcript-pool composition rather than TPM-quantified expression, with approximate relative transcript abundance biased by assembly quality.
quote: - **Metatranscriptome KO from contig annotations** is *transcript-pool composition*, not TPM-quantified expression. Contig-level annotation count ≈ relative transcript abundance, but is biased by assembly quality.
heading: Limitations

text: The Harvard Forest report excludes quantitative metabolomics, NOM, and proteomics because it excludes nmdc_arkin tables, although equivalent quantitative layers exist in nmdc_arkin.{nom_gold, metabolomics_gold, proteomics_gold}.
quote: - **No quantitative metabolomics, NOM, or proteomics** because the project excludes `nmdc_arkin` tables. Equivalent quantitative layers exist in `nmdc_arkin.{nom_gold, metabolomics_gold, proteomics_gold}` and could be added if scope expands.
heading: Limitations

text: Harvard Forest abiotic_features are all zeros because of a study-specific NMDC parsing artifact, leaving no soil temperature, pH, or nitrogen measurements in the KBase Data Lakehouse and only the +5°C treatment label as an environmental contrast.
quote: - **`abiotic_features` is all zeros** for these samples (NMDC parsing artifact for this specific study) — no in-lakehouse soil temperature, pH, or nitrogen measurements. The +5°C treatment label is the only environmental contrast.
heading: Limitations

text: All Harvard Forest organic-horizon DNA samples are lab-incubated because the NMDC pipeline did not produce direct organic DNA, preventing clean separation of incubation in the organic-horizon DNA analysis.
quote: - **Organic-horizon DNA samples are all lab-incubated**; direct organic DNA was not produced by the NMDC pipeline. This makes it impossible to factor incubation cleanly out of the DNA pool's organic-horizon analysis.
